items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A human-centred worldview in which humans manage the environment sustainably for human benefit, often through regulation, taxes and incentives"?
items.answer: anthropocentrism
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of anthropocentrism.

items.stem: Explain how an EVS can be understood as a system.
items.answer: It has inputs (education, culture, religion, media, peers, experience), processes (thinking, weighing evidence), and outputs (decisions, actions, voting, consumer choices), with feedback as experiences reinforce or change values.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It has inputs (education, culture, religion, media, peers, experience), processes (thinking, weighing evidence), and outputs (decisions, actions, voting, consumer choices), with feedback as experiences reinforce or change values. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Amara writes: "A person's EVS is fixed for life." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: EVSs change with education, experience, media, culture and events (e.g. a disaster or travel can shift views).
items.markingKey: EVSs change with education, experience, media, culture and events (e.g. a disaster or travel can shift views). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identify the EVS shown by each statement: (i) "Nuclear fusion will give us unlimited clean energy." (ii) "A carbon tax will make polluters pay." (iii) "Rivers have the right to flow freely."
items.answer: (i) technocentric (cornucopian) (ii) anthropocentric (environmental manager) (iii) ecocentric (deep ecology / rights of nature).
items.markingKey: (i) technocentric (cornucopian) (ii) anthropocentric (environmental manager) (iii) ecocentric (deep ecology / rights of nature).

items.stem: Explain a technocentric EVS, referring in detail to the Three Gorges Dam, China and to at least one other example you have studied. [7]
items.answer: The dam (completed 2006, 22.5 GW) displaced about 1.3 million people to provide hydroelectricity and flood control. Large-scale engineering was trusted to meet energy needs and control nature for economic growth. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The dam (completed 2006, 22.5 GW) displaced about 1.3 million people to provide hydroelectricity and flood control. Large-scale engineering was trusted to meet energy needs and control nature for economic growth. items.stem: Briefly analyse two contrasting points of view on the statement: "An ecocentric value system is unrealistic in a world of eight billion people."
items.answer: Pure ecocentrism is hard to implement at scale, but ecocentric principles are increasingly embedded in policy and are needed to avoid overshoot.
items.markingKey: For: billions depend on intensive agriculture and energy use. Against: ecocentric practices (agroecology, Indigenous land management) sustain productivity. [4]: [1] for a valid argument for and [1] for its development; [1] for a valid argument against and [1] for its development; generic points with no environmental context are capped at [2].

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "intrinsic value"?
options: The value something has in itself, independent of its usefulness to humans
Cumulative knowledge of relationships between living things and their environment, held by Indigenous and local communities
The social and political movement, growing from the 1960s, that seeks to protect the environment through awareness, lobbying, legislation and direct action
The 1987 UN report "Our Common Future" that defined sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
items.answer: The value something has in itself, independent of its usefulness to humans
items.markingKey: A. "intrinsic value" is the value something has in itself, independent of its usefulness to humans.

items.stem: Briefly explain why EVSs are said to lie on a spectrum rather than in fixed categories.
items.answer: Most people hold mixed views that vary with issue and context (e.g. supporting renewables but also wilderness protection); positions shade from deep ecologist and self-reliance soft ecologist through environmental manager to cornucopian.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Most people hold mixed views that vary with issue and context (e.g. supporting renewables but also wilderness protection); positions shade from deep ecologist and self-reliance soft ecologist through environmental manager to cornucopian. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Compare a cornucopian with a deep ecologist.
items.answer: A cornucopian sees resources as effectively unlimited through technology and markets; a deep ecologist gives nature equal value to humans and argues for reducing human impact and population.
items.markingKey: A cornucopian sees resources as effectively unlimited through technology and markets; a deep ecologist gives nature equal value to humans and argues for reducing human impact and population. [1] per valid, explicit comparison up to [3].

items.stem: Distinguish between a deep ecologist and a cornucopian.
items.answer: A cornucopian sees resources as effectively unlimited through technology and markets; a deep ecologist gives nature equal value to humans and argues for reducing human impact and population.
items.markingKey: A cornucopian sees resources as effectively unlimited through technology and markets; a deep ecologist gives nature equal value to humans and argues for reducing human impact and population. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between technocentrism and ecocentrism.
items.answer: Ecocentrism puts nature first, values self-restraint and small-scale, low-impact solutions and distrusts technology; technocentrism trusts human ingenuity and technology to solve problems and sustain growth.
items.markingKey: Ecocentrism puts nature first, values self-restraint and small-scale, low-impact solutions and distrusts technology; technocentrism trusts human ingenuity and technology to solve problems and sustain growth. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.answer: The dam (completed 2006, 22.5 GW) displaced about 1.3 million people to provide hydroelectricity and flood control. Large-scale engineering was trusted to meet energy needs and control nature for economic growth.

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "An ecocentric value system is unrealistic in a world of eight billion people."
items.answer: Pure ecocentrism is hard to implement at scale, but ecocentric principles are increasingly embedded in policy and are needed to avoid overshoot.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Brundtland Report"?
options: The value something has in itself, independent of its usefulness to humans
A nature-centred worldview that gives intrinsic value to all life and ecosystems, emphasises self-restraint and minimal disturbance of natural processes, and distrusts large-scale technology
The legal principle that ecosystems or natural entities have rights of their own, as recognised in Ecuador's 2008 constitution
The 1987 UN report "Our Common Future" that defined sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
items.answer: The 1987 UN report "Our Common Future" that defined sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
items.markingKey: D. "Brundtland Report" is the 1987 UN report "Our Common Future" that defined sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.

items.stem: Outline how major disasters have shaped the environmental movement.
items.answer: Disasters such as Minamata, Bhopal, Chernobyl and the Exxon Valdez gave vivid evidence of harm, generated media coverage and public anger, and led to new laws, institutions and international agreements.
items.markingKey: Disasters such as Minamata, Bhopal, Chernobyl and the Exxon Valdez gave vivid evidence of harm, generated media coverage and public anger, and led to new laws, institutions and international agreements. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: "Environmental disasters only lead to local changes." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Disasters often trigger national laws and international agreements, e.g. Minamata led to the Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013).
items.markingKey: Disasters often trigger national laws and international agreements, e.g. Minamata led to the Minamata Convention on Mercury (2013). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: An NGO is independent, campaigns and can use direct action or lobbying but cannot make law; a government agency (e.g. the US EPA) has legal authority to regulate and enforce.

items.answer: Individuals often start change by shifting values, but lasting impact depends on governments translating it into law and policy.

items.stem: Distinguish between community-based conservation and fortress conservation.
items.answer: Fortress conservation excludes local people from protected areas; community-based conservation involves local and Indigenous people in management and benefits (e.g. Namibian conservancies).
items.markingKey: Fortress conservation excludes local people from protected areas; community-based conservation involves local and Indigenous people in management and benefits (e.g. Namibian conservancies). items.stem: Outline how cultural burning in northern Australia contributes to climate-change mitigation.
items.answer: Early dry-season cool burns reduce the area burnt by hot late fires, cutting greenhouse-gas emissions; Indigenous groups earn carbon credits under the Savanna Fire Management method.
items.markingKey: Early dry-season cool burns reduce the area burnt by hot late fires, cutting greenhouse-gas emissions; Indigenous groups earn carbon credits under the Savanna Fire Management method.

items.answer: Indigenous fire knowledge reduces destructive late-season fires and maintains habitat mosaics, while owners keep cultural ties to country.

items.stem: With reference to the resource booklet and examples you have studied, evaluate the claim: "Granting legal rights to nature is the most effective way to protect ecosystems."
items.answer: Rights of nature are a powerful symbolic and legal tool but need enforcement and integration with other policies to be effective.
items.markingKey: Strengths / supporting points: gives ecosystems standing in court (Whanganui, Ecuador); shifts values towards ecocentrism. Conclusion: Rights of nature are a powerful symbolic and legal tool but need enforcement and integration with other policies to be effective. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "stewardship"?

The value something has in itself, independent of its usefulness to humans
The value something has because it is useful to humans, e.g. timber, food or recreation
The 1987 UN report "Our Common Future" that defined sustainable development as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
items.answer: The responsible care and management of the environment on behalf of others and future generations
items.markingKey: A. "stewardship" is the responsible care and management of the environment on behalf of others and future generations.

items.stem: Explain why Silent Spring was so influential.
items.answer: It used scientific evidence in accessible language to show that DDT biomagnified, thinning eggshells of birds of prey; it raised public awareness, challenged industry and led to the US DDT ban (1972) and the creation of the EPA (1970).

items.stem: Explain why conflicts can arise between conservation projects and Indigenous peoples.
items.answer: "Fortress conservation" has removed people from protected areas, denying access to land and resources; outside priorities may ignore Indigenous rights, knowledge and consent.

items.stem: Outline the role of social media in the modern environmental movement.
items.answer: It spreads information and images rapidly, allows global coordination (e.g. Fridays for Future strikes from 2018 involving millions), gives a voice to young people and Indigenous groups, but can also spread misinformation.

items.stem: Explain why Indigenous land management is often associated with high biodiversity.
items.answer: Long-term, place-based knowledge and customary rules limit over-harvesting; practices such as rotational farming and cultural burning maintain habitat mosaics; secure land tenure resists deforestation (e.g. Indigenous territories in the Brazilian Amazon have lower deforestation rates).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Long-term, place-based knowledge and customary rules limit over-harvesting; practices such as rotational farming and cultural burning maintain habitat mosaics; secure land tenure resists deforestation (e.g. Indigenous territories in the Brazilian Amazon have lower deforestation rates). Survey of 200 students at an international school: "Which statement best matches your view?" Technology will solve environmental problems 34%; Governments should regulate and tax pollution 41%; Humans must consume less and respect nature's rights 25%.

items.stem: Distinguish between a cornucopian and a deep ecologist.
items.answer: A cornucopian sees resources as effectively unlimited through technology and markets; a deep ecologist gives nature equal value to humans and argues for reducing human impact and population.

items.stem: Distinguish between Western scientific knowledge and traditional ecological knowledge.
items.answer: TEK is holistic, place-based, built over generations and often transmitted orally and through practice; Western science is based on hypothesis testing, controlled measurement and peer review, and seeks generalisable laws. They can complement each other.
